Sahil Aggarwal 11 min read · Oct 21, 2026 -- 2 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size What changes when a product feature works perfectly in testing but delivers inconsistent or incorrect results once customers start using it? That is one of the challenges Product Managers face when building AI-powered products. According to McKinsey’s 2025 State of AI survey , 88% of respondents said their organizations used AI in at least one business function. Yet, only 7% reported that AI had been fully scaled across their organizations ( Source ). These self-reported findings highlight the gap between AI adoption and operational maturity. For Product Managers, that gap raises new questions about feasibility, output quality, reliability, and measurable business value. Traditional product-management principles still apply, but AI changes how teams define requirements, prioritize features, evaluate results, and manage products after launch. In this blog, I, Sahil Aggarwal , will explain how AI changes traditional product-management practices, from defining requirements and prioritizing features to evaluating performance, managing uncertainty, and measuring product success. AI Product Manager vs Traditional Product Manager: Key Differences Both roles focus on customer needs, product strategy, and business outcomes. However, AI-powered products introduce additional considerations around model behavior, evaluation, technical feasibility, and operating costs, changing how Product Managers make decisions throughout the product lifecycle. Press enter or click to view image in full size What Doesn’t Change in AI Product Management? AI does not change the fundamental purpose of product management. Customer discovery, strategic prioritization, stakeholder collaboration, and delivering measurable business value remain essential. What changes is the additional evidence and technical judgment required to make reliable product decisions. This also raises questions about what AI Product Managers should own versus the decisions shared with technical teams. Press enter or click to view image in full size How Does AI Change Product Discovery and Problem Validation? What if customers want an AI feature, but the technology cannot reliably deliver the outcome they expect? This is where AI product discovery requires a different approach. Customer interviews and market research may confirm demand, but they cannot establish whether an AI system can perform the intended task at an acceptable quality level. Product Managers therefore need to test technical assumptions alongside user needs before committing to development. How to Validate AI Feasibility Before Development An effective AI discovery process introduces three practical steps: Establish a baseline : Measure how users currently complete the task, including completion time, accuracy, and common frustrations. This provides a benchmark against which the proposed AI feature can be evaluated. Test representative scenarios : Build a limited prototype and evaluate it against realistic inputs, including ambiguous requests, incomplete information, and unusual cases. The objective is to uncover capability limitations early, not perfect the product. Validate with actual users : Observe whether the prototype produces useful outcomes in the intended workflow. A technically impressive demonstration does not necessarily improve how customers complete their tasks. Consider a customer support platform where users struggle to find answers to account-related questions. Instead of immediately committing to an AI assistant, the Product Manager first measures how often customers fail to find information through existing search and support workflows. The team then tests an AI prototype against a sample of actual customer questions, checking whether it retrieves relevant information and provides useful responses. If the prototype struggles with account-specific requests, the PM might narrow the initial scope to general support questions rather than launch a broader assistant.
